sequences.text: [organ music playing] Welcome to Radio City Music Hall. It’s time. Any questions? No. Walk with me. [eerie organ music playing] [mechanical whirring] [audience applauding and cheering] Good evening. Hi, I’m John Mulaney, nice to meet you. Jon Brion, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for coming to see me at Radio City Music Hall. I love to play venues where if the guy that built the venue could see me on the stage, he would be a little bit bummed about it. Look at this. This is so much nicer than what I’m about to do. It’s really… It’s really tragic. What a historic and beautiful and deeply haunted building this is. I keep walking through cold spots being like, “I wonder who that used to be.” I’ve never seen a ghost, by the way. I asked my mom if she’d ever seen a ghost. That’s where we’re at conversation-wise in our relationship as a mother and son, because I’m 35 and I don’t have any children to talk about and she doesn’t understand my career. So I was home for Christmas and we were just eating Triscuits in silence and I was staring at the floor and I was like, “Well, here goes nothing. ‘You ever seen a ghost?'” And my mom said, “Yes.” Which is the best answer. She said, “I never told you this before but our house, when you were growing up, was haunted.” I said, “Say more right now!” She said, “Outside you and your brother’s room, I used to see the ghost of a little girl in a Victorian nightgown and then she would walk down the hallway and then she would evaporate.” And then my dad said, “Let’s change the subject!” And I think he was just doing that dad-thing of, like, “This is a weird topic and I want to talk about a book I read about World War II.” But the way it came off was that he definitely killed that little girl. “Let’s change the subject! Why are we even talking about Penelope… or whatever her name was? I didn’t kill her! Whoever did kill her only did it to protect her from this world.” None of us really know our fathers. Anyway… My dad is so weird. I’d love to meet him someday. You know, my friend was telling me that his dad used to beat him with a belt and that’s just the setup to my story, so… Forget about that poor son of a bitch. Anyway… He was talking and I was waiting for him to be done so I could talk. So he’s “talk, talk, talk.” It’s my turn next! And… [audience laughing] I said, “My dad never hit us.” My dad is a lawyer and he was a debate team champion.

gold_monopoly_bit:
I try to make it seem like I'm just getting this out, but I know
all the moves, I know every little piece of it.

[0:05] One... Two... Three... It's just here, just go here.

[0:15] This is what a Louis C. K. joke looks like. It's a short
one, only 207 words.

[0:21] But they're 207 words that are chosen very purposefully,
practiced until every one counts for something.

[0:28] Today I want to go through this joke beat by beat, and
explore how Louis C. K. constructs and performs his comedy.

[0:37] My girls are six and nine now. They're actually a really
exciting age because they're learning to do some cool stuff.

[0:42] Every joke has to have a premise, an idea that the inevitable
punch line will snap comedically into place.

[0:50] The premise should be really clear, whether it's implied as
in some one-liners or stated outright.

[0:56] As Chris Rock once said, "A lot of comedians have great
jokes, and they don't... why isn't this working? It's not working
because the audience does not understand the premise."

[1:05] In this case the premise has two parts, accomplished in two
sentences.

[1:09] First, Louis is playing monopoly with his daughters, and
second—

[1:27] The second part of this premise is beautifully structured.

[1:30] Because besides very lucidly delivering the premise that this
joke is going to be how a six-year-old girl learns what it means to
lose in Monopoly—

[1:37] Louis actually gets some laughs out of the sentence by the
addition of a couple words and a strategic rhythm.

[1:44] I mean the simplest way to end the sentence is to say that
she's not emotionally developed enough to handle losing at Monopoly,

[1:51] But instead, he says, "to handle her." In this way Louis adds
two little comedic surprises in the premise, and makes sure to include
a pause so that each can be appreciated in their own beat.

[2:06] "To handle her." Comedians like Louis C.K. are experienced
enough to master not only their own delivery, but where the laughs
will occur in their jokes, and how to deal with them.

[2:26] Telling a joke is like riding a wave of feeling, and if you
watch Louis C.K.'s comedy, you'll see that during laughs what he does
is emphasize his last line.

[2:35] It doesn't give the audience new information.

[2:38] He augments the information just given — something he actually
learned how to do brilliantly from Jerry Seinfeld.

[2:44] "I'm opening for Jerry in front of like twelve hundred or
twenty-five hundred people, and people are applauding bits. And I had
never encountered that. I didn't know how to handle it. I asked Jerry
what to do, and he said, 'You stay in the bit.' You stay in the bit
they're reacting to."

[3:01] If you're angry and that's why they're applauding, you stay
in that energy. Because the Monopoly loss is dark. It's heavy.

[3:11] It's not like... the choice of Candyland here, though Louis
acts as if it was pulled out of thin air, is the perfect counterpoint
to Monopoly.

[3:28] It's visual. The game pops straight into your mind as an
object of colourful innocence. The dramatization and the funny voices
are also performed like they were spontaneously made up.

[3:37] But the words and the images he uses — like "fudgy thing" and
"gummy twirly-o's" — are carefully chosen to enhance that visual sense.

[3:46] Louis is never not in control. And that's important, because
since the premise has been so strongly set up and the counterpoint
drawn out so vividly—

[3:55] The laughs that Louis gets here are actually laughs in
anticipation of a punchline not yet said.

[4:01] The audience is already imagining how dark the Monopoly loss
is going to be.

[4:06] Just watch how he gradually increases these anticipatory
laughs, like the audience is a fiddle, to the final three-word punchline.

[4:32] "Gotta give it all to me. Give it to me. That's right."

[4:36] One thing Louis doesn't get recognized for enough, in my
opinion, is his ability to dramatize in his jokes.

[4:42] When he acts out this conversation with his daughter, the
light touch he gives — especially with that hand movement right on
the punchline — really locks the audience into the space where he
wants them to be.

[4:52] The audience needs to see this situation from a six-year-old
perspective for it to work.

[4:56] And if he succeeds, the tags — the two additional punchlines
that follow — will be that much more devastating and hilarious.

[5:16] "You're going down hard. It's really bad."

[5:18] Casting the audience in the perspective of a six-year-old is
important for another reason, because I think on a deeper level Louis
is actually trying to make a comment here

[5:27] On the actual ruthlessness of the economy we live in, where
property really is taken away from people, sometimes by monopolistic
interests with debt to spare.

[5:38] That's the thing his daughter is not emotionally developed
enough to comprehend.

[5:42] And when we see it through her eyes, the reality seems even
darker than it usually does.

[5:48] Especially in the final tag.

[6:08] You know, more than anything else, I think I'm obsessed with
articulation, with the magic of putting things just the right way.

[6:15] There are 207 words in this joke, and not a single one is
wasted. They're used either in meaning or in rhythm to contribute to
the overall effect — an effect that lets us see the world from a
different angle, and more importantly, makes us laugh.

[6:30] Like great poetry, great stand-up comedy is language distilled
to its most potent form.

[6:36] And these days, few people distill it better than Louis C.K.
